text:
August was drawing to a close, and they were already dining by lamplight, the doors open onto the green sunset where a spindle of rosy copper still floated. The deserted sea, a swallow’s blue-black, slept, and when the diners fell silent, one could hear the small, weary, regular wash of the neap tides. Among the shadows, Philippe sought Vinca’s gaze, to test the strength of that invisible thread which had bound them to one another for so many years and preserved them, exalted and pure, from the melancholy that weighs upon the ends of meals, the ends of seasons, the ends of days. But she lowered her eyes to her plate, and the light from the hanging lamp polished her rounded eyelids, her round brown cheeks, her little chin. Then he felt abandoned and sought—beyond the lion-shaped peninsula that jutted out over the sea, crowned by three trembling stars—the road, white in the night, that led to Ker-Anna. A few hours more, a little more blue ash in this sky that the sunset tinged with dawn, a few more ritual phrases: “Well, well, ten o’clock already. Children, you don’t seem to realize that here one goes to bed at ten?” “And yet I haven’t done anything out of the ordinary, Madame Audebert; well, I feel as tired as if I hadn’t stopped...” A few more clinks of crockery, the hard clatter of dominoes on the bare table, one more moaning protest from Lisette who, three-quarters asleep, would refuse to go to bed... One more attempt to win back the gaze, the inward smile, the trust of the mysteriously wounded Vinca, and the hour would strike, the same hour that, the night before, had seen Philippe steal away... He thought of it without any precise desire, without any plan, and as though compelled by Vinca’s mood to retreat toward another refuge, another gentle shoulder, an efficacious warmth, urgently needed by this convalescent from pleasure, wounded besides by the passionate hostility of an adolescent...

The rites were performed, one by one; a servant carried away the whimpering Lisette, and Madame Ferret placed the double six on the gleaming table.

“Are you coming outside, Vinca? These silkworm moths banging into all the lamps are unbearable...”

She followed him without answering, and near the sea they still found that light which twilight leaves there for so long.

“Don’t you want me to go and fetch your scarf?”

“No, thank you.”

They walked together, bathed in a very light blue mist that rose from the salt meadow and smelled of wild thyme. Philippe restrained himself from taking his friend’s arm, and was appalled by his own discretion.

“My God, what is there between us? Are we lost to one another? Since she knows nothing of what happened over there, perhaps I have only to forget it, and we shall become happy again as before, unhappy as before, united as before?”

But he did not add hypnotic faith to his wish, since Vinca walked beside him, cold and gentle as though her great love had left her, and she did not perceive her companion’s anguish. Besides, Phil felt the hour drawing near and suffered from a quivering like the fever he had the day after, stung by a weever fish, he had felt in his bandaged arm the burning that the rising tide reawakened there...

He stopped and wiped his forehead:

“I’m suffocating. I don’t feel well, Vinca.”

“Oh! no, not well,” Vinca’s voice echoed.

He thought it a truce and eagerly reached toward her with voice and gesture:

“Oh! you’re so sweet! Oh! darling!...”

“No,” the voice interrupted, “I’m not sweet.”

The childish sentence left Philippe some hope, and he seized his friend’s bare arm.

“You’re angry with me, I know, for having cried today like a woman...”

“No, not like a woman...”

He blushed in the darkness and tried to explain himself:

“You understand, that conger eel you were tormenting in its hole... That creature’s blood on your lobster hook... It suddenly turned my stomach...”

“Ah! yes, your stomach... turned...”

The tone of her voice was so knowing that Philippe held his breath in fear. “She knows everything.” He waited for the crushing account and the explosion of tears and reproaches. But Vinca remained silent, and after a long while, as after the calm pause that follows a thunderbolt, he ventured a timid question:

“And is that weakness enough to make you seem as though you no longer love me?”

Vinca turned toward him the pale, hazy patch of her face, confined between the two rigid hedges of her hair:

“Oh! Phil, I still love you. Unfortunately, that changes nothing.”

He felt his leaping heart strike his throat:

“Yes? Then you’re going to forgive me for having been such a ‘little girl,’ so ridiculous?”

She hesitated for only a second:

“Why, yes. I’m going to forgive you, Phil. But that, too, changes nothing.”

“About what?”

“About us, Phil.”

She spoke with a sibylline gentleness which he did not dare question further and in which he did not dare rejoice. Vinca must have followed him in his mental retreat, for she added subtly:

“Do you remember the scenes you used to make with me, and the ones I made with you, not three weeks ago, because we were impatient at having four years, five years, to languish before getting married?... My poor Phil, I really think I would like to go backward and become a child again, today...”

He waited for her to emphasize, to comment upon that skillful, insidious “today” suspended before him in the pure blue air of the August night. But Vinca already knew how to arm herself with silence. He insisted:

“Then you’re not angry with me anymore? Tomorrow, we shall be... we shall be Vinca and Phil, as always? Forever?”

“Forever, if you want, Phil... Come. Let’s go back inside. It’s cool.”

She had not repeated “as always” after him. But he contented himself with that incomplete oath and with the cold little hand clasped for a moment in his own. For at that instant, the unwinding chain of the well, the alarm-bell clang of the empty bucket against the curb, the scraping of curtains along their rod in an open window—the day’s last human sounds—rang out the hour for Philippe, the same hour for which he had watched the night before, in order to reopen the villa door and dart out in secret... Ah! the muted red light of an unknown room... Ah! the dark happiness, death attained by degrees, life regained by slow beats of the wings...

As though, since the night before, he had been awaiting a sort of absolution from Vinca—an ambiguous absolution which she had just granted him with such sincerity in her tone, such reticence in her words—he suddenly assessed, as a man, the gift that a beautiful, imperious demoness had bestowed upon him.




XIV


“Has the date of your departure for Paris been settled?” Madame Dalleray asked.

“We are still due to go back on September twenty-fifth,” Philippe replied. “Sometimes, depending on where the Sundays fall in the month, our departure falls on the twenty-third or twenty-fourth, or the twenty-sixth. But it rarely varies by more than two days.”

“Yes... In short, you are leaving in a fortnight. In a fortnight, at this time...”

Philippe tore his gaze from the sea, flat and white near the sands, in the distance the color of a tuna’s back beneath the low clouds, and turned in astonishment toward Madame Dalleray. Wrapped in ample white cloth like the dress of the women of Tahiti, she smoked gravely, her hair impeccably arranged, powdered with a powder the same color as her skin, and nothing about her revealed that this young man seated not far from her, handsome and dark like her, was anything to her other than a younger brother.
